messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Event Recall: Talking about the event, Event Involvement: People who are related to the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mikaere had spent most of his life on building sites, the kind of work where he knew how to read a room quickly and where to put his hands, and at 63 he still moved with the habits of a man used to measuring risk in concrete ways. Since his wife died, he had lived alone, and the silence of the evenings had become more noticeable over time. When he came to therapy, he spoke in a flat, careful voice and said that the hardest period in his life began years earlier, during a relationship that had turned physically abusive. The details he offered came out slowly, but the account was clear enough: there had been repeated moments when his partner used her hands against him, and what stayed with him most were the body parts involved, especially the hands and arms that he could not stop noticing even now. He remembered not just being struck, but the humiliating closeness of it, the sense that those parts of her body had become impossible to see without feeling his chest tighten. At the time, he had told almost no one. He stayed, kept working, and tried to handle it on his own, telling himself he could manage if he did not make a fuss.

Afterward, even ordinary conversations began to carry a charge for him if they touched on what had happened. When someone asked direct questions about that relationship, or when a story came up involving abuse, Mikaere would feel his jaw lock and his mind go blank in a way that made him want to change the subject immediately. He avoided talking about it with anyone, including family, and he was especially uneasy around people connected to the relationship, even indirectly, because their presence seemed to pull him back into the same helplessness. He found himself arranging his days so he would stay near exits, whether he was in a pub, a waiting room, or a shop. On the job, he preferred positions where he could see the door and keep his back clear, and he noticed that if a meeting or tool-box talk became tense, he would say little and look for a way out rather than risk disagreement. He had come to believe that any confrontation could turn into something he would not be able to handle, and that belief shaped his choices in small but persistent ways. Over the years, he also began spending money impulsively after difficult moments, buying things he did not need, almost as if the act of spending could drown out what he was feeling for a while. He did not describe it as pleasure; it was more like a brief distraction or comfort that left him with regret once the moment passed.

His sense of danger remained active in the present. Mikaere said he jumped at ordinary sounds that other people barely seemed to notice: a dropped hammer, a car backfiring near the site, a door slamming in the hallway of his apartment building. Those noises made his body react before he could think. At night, he would wake and check that he was safe, sometimes sitting up in the dark and listening, then getting out of bed to look through the apartment before settling down again. He also scanned exits as soon as he entered any room or building, a habit so automatic that he often caught himself studying doorways before he had even taken off his hat. In crowded stores or job meetings, he watched who was near the doors and where he could move if he needed to. These routines had become part of how he moved through the world, and he seemed tired by the effort of maintaining them.

When he spoke about himself, the harshest judgments were directed inward. Mikaere said, with visible shame, that he could not rely on himself. He described times when he had wanted to stand up for himself or leave and had not done so, and he interpreted that as proof that he was a weak person. He did not speak of those years with anger so much as with a resigned disappointment in himself, as though he had failed some test that other men would have passed. He also said that he felt dead inside. He did not mean this dramatically; he meant that there were stretches of the day when he could function mechanically but felt cut off from warmth or ease. At work, he still showed up and did the job, but he did so with a kind of internal distance that worried him. In recent months, the combination of waking at night, scanning every room, avoiding any disagreement, and feeling increasingly hollow had become harder to manage. What brought him in now was the sense that he could no longer keep pretending he was fine. He was most afraid that he would remain trapped in this watchful, empty state for the rest of his life, and most hoping that he might learn how to feel safe enough to stop living as if danger were always just beyond the next doorway.
